OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the causes of morbidity and mortality in polytrauma patients.
Assess resuscitation needs to guide the initial treatment of polytrauma patients.
Discuss the an orthopaedic evaluation and initial treatment of polytrauma patients.
Review the concepts of damage-control orthopaedics and early appropriate treatment in
polytrauma patients.
Overview
Definition
A polytrauma patient is any patient with a combination of multiple system injury and an injury
severity score (ISS) of 16 or higher.

Epidemiology
Injury is the leading cause of death for Americans 45 years and younger and is the leading
cause of years of life lost.1 Injury is the fourth leading cause of death for Americans of any
age.1
In 2013, the estimated cost for injuries and work-loss in the United States was $671 billion.2
In the United States, 214,000 people die from injury each year (1 person every 3 minutes).1
Motor vehicle collisions and falls account for substantial morbidity and mortality in the United
States each year. In 2015, motor vehicle collisions accounted for 35,000 fatalities. Yearly, 2.8
million people are treated in emergency departments for injuries from falls.1

Mortality and the Golden Hour
Three peak times of death occur after trauma4
Within minutes—Approximately 50% of deaths after trauma occur within minutes, from a
massive head or chest injury or hemorrhage.
Within the first few days—Approximately 30% of deaths after trauma occur within the first
few days after injury, most commonly from a neurologic injury.

Days to weeks after injury—Approximately 20% of deaths after trauma occur days to weeks
after injury because of infection and/or multiple organ failure.

Mortality and the Golden Hour
The golden hour refers to the initial 60 minutes immediately after life-threatening injury;
the concept was popularized by R. Adams Cowley to provide a sense of urgency for
proper trauma care.5 Traumatic brain injury and uncontrolled hemorrhage are the major
causes of mortality within the first hour after trauma. Appropriate intervention in this
period avoids mortality observed in the middle and late peaks and limits morbidity.
Trauma Scoring Systems
Components of current scoring systems include physiologic data, anatomic data, a
combination of the two, and more specialized data.
Although no single scoring system has been universally adopted, each has advantages and
disadvantages.
Glasgow Coma Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale attempts to score the function (level of consciousness) of the central
nervous system. The sum of scores for eye opening, verbal response, and motor response is
the total score6 (Table 2).
For intubated patients, the verbal score is eliminated, and the score is modified with a “T” after
the numeric score.

Injury Severity Score
The sum of the squares of the three highest AIS scores of six regions provides an overall
severity score. The regions are the head and neck, face, thorax (including the thoracic spine),
abdomen (including the lumbar spine), extremities and pelvis, and external (skin).7
Each region is scored on a scale from 1 (minor injury) to 6 (almost always fatal).
Any region with an AIS score of 6 is automatically assigned an ISS value of 75, which represents
a nonsurvivable injury.
A score of 16 or higher frequently is used as the definition of major trauma and correlates with
mortality in an age-dependent fashion.
Because the ISS scores only one injury per body region, the ISS does not reflect patient
morbidity associated with multiple lower extremity fractures.8
New ISS
This modification of the ISS sums the squares of the AIS scores of the three most substantial
injuries, even if they occur in the same anatomic area.9
Better predictor of survival than the ISS
A study assessing orthopaedic polytrauma patients found the New ISS to be superior to the ISS
with regard to predicting hospital length of stay and length of admission in the intensive care
unit (ICU).10
Trauma and Injury Severity Score
The Trauma and Injury Severity Score predicts mortality based on postinjury anatomic and
physiologic abnormalities.11
Uses age, the Revised Trauma Score (calculated in the emergency department), the ISS
(calculated using discharge diagnosis), and whether the mechanism of injury was blunt or
penetrating
Data from any institution can be compared with mortality data from the Major Trauma
Outcomes Study conducted by the American College of Surgeons in 1990.


Trauma Scoring Systems
The ISS and AIS are the most used injury scoring systems for trauma patients; however, a
weakness of these scores is that only the highest scoring injury per system is included
for that system in the ISS, even more than one exists. For example, the ISS does not
score bilateral femur fractures, which historically have been associated with a mortality
rate as high as 40% and have been an independent risk factor for pulmonary
compromise8 (Resource 1).
Prehospital Care and Field Triage
General Principles
Rapid assessment: rapid assessment to identify life-threatening injuries4
Appropriate interventions: appropriate interventions to address life-threatening conditions
(airway, breathing, circulation, external hemorrhage control); the goal of prehospital care is to
minimize preventable deaths.
Rapid transport: rapid transport to an appropriate facility based on the patient’s injuries
Specific criteria for transport to a trauma center may vary by state and region; however, the
goal is to transport the most acute patients to the highest-acuity centers.
Recommendations of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for transport to high-
acuity centers include the following12:
Systolic blood pressure lower than 90 mm Hg
Respiratory rate lower than 10 bpm or higher than 29 bmp
Glasgow Coma Scale score less than 14
Paralysis
Open skull fracture
Amputation
Pelvic fracture
Mangled extremity
Two or more long bone fractures
Flail chest
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003016
7/35

In addition, patients with the following mechanisms of injury should be considered for
transport to high-acuity centers12:
Penetrating chest or abdominal trauma
Falls from a height of more than 20 ft
Motorcycle collisions and crashes, high-velocity motor vehicle collisions
Patient factors, including pregnancy and dialysis dependence, also should be considered.12

General Principles
Rapidity of transport is critical because approximately 50% of mortality occurs within the
first hour. The first prehospital evaluation is the initial primary survey of a patient. The
goals are to identify life-threatening injuries, secure the most critical body systems, and
conduct early transport to appropriate facilities. Trauma systems have evolved to quickly
direct patients to facilities equipped to treat them. Continuous oversight, quality
improvement, and system analysis and refinement have led to outstanding patient care
and improved outcomes in polytrauma patients at high-volume trauma centers.13
Time to transport from the field to a trauma center is critical. Transport should not be
delayed to start fluids. Prehospital blood product transfusions have not been shown to
decrease mortality rates compared with non–blood product volume replacement in the
prehospital setting.
Conversely, splinting of extremities with obvious fractures before transport provides
comfort while limiting additional injury. Based on military experience, field application of
tourniquets for mangled limbs and amputations controls blood loss and has become
accepted in many communities. Some communities also have adopted field application
of pelvic binders with the same rationale.
Initial Hospital Workup and Resuscitation
Goals

Diagnosis and management of life-threatening injuries takes priority over a sequential,
detailed, definitive workup.
Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol, which provides a systematic method to
evaluate trauma patients, was developed to teach this concept and ultimately improve patient
survival.
Components of ATLS
Primary survey
A systematic effort to identify life-threatening injuries immediately
Treatment and resuscitation are performed simultaneously as problems are identified.
Consists of evaluation of the ABCDEs—airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure—
which may need to be repeated because of the evolving nature of patient injuries and patient
response.
Chest and AP pelvic radiographs should be obtained in all patients who sustain blunt trauma
to identify potential life-threatening sources of bleeding.
Treatment related to evaluation of circulation include the placement of tourniquets for
hemorrhage control with uncontrolled extremity bleeding and circumferential pelvic
compression with the use of a pelvic sheet or binder for volume-expanding pelvic ring
disruption.
Extremity trauma
Bleeding associated with fractures may be life threatening.
Circumferential pelvic compression with the use of pelvic binders or sheets currently is
recommended for patients in whom pelvic ring disruption and shock are suspected.
External hemorrhage is controlled via direct pressure. Extremity tourniquets for severe
bleeding associated with open fractures decrease mortality.
Immobilization of the extremity helps control internal bleeding. Gross correction of obvious
deformities also helps improve tissue perfusion and lessens ongoing soft-tissue compromise.
A traction splint can be used in patients in whom femur fractures are suspected because it
stabilizes the fracture and controls pain. A traction splint is contraindicated in patients with
obvious knee injuries or deformities.
Amputations
Tourniquets are used to control bleeding and can be applied in the field or on arrival to the
hospital.
The amputated parts are cleaned by rinsing them with the use of lactated Ringer solution.

The parts are covered with sterile gauze moistened with lactated Ringer solution and placed
in a plastic bag.
The bag is labeled and placed in another container filled with ice.
The part must not be allowed to freeze or be immersed directly in an aqueous medium.
The part is transported with the patient.
Initial Assessment

Initial Assessment
Initial assessment should be rapid and systematic. Patients with potentially life-
threatening injuries must be quickly recognized and transported to the closest
appropriate hospital. Definitive management of internal hemorrhage cannot be
provided at the scene. Mechanisms of injury that may result in major injuries include
falls from a height of more than 15 feet; motor vehicle collisions in which a fatality has
occurred, a passenger has been ejected, or extrication has taken longer than 20 minutes;
motor pedestrian collisions; motorcycle collisions in which the vehicle was traveling
faster than 20 mph; and penetrating injury in the area of vital structures (knife or
gunshot wound).4
Primary Survey

Primary Survey
The initial assessment begins with the primary survey. The primary survey assesses the
ABCDEs. This assessment is performed exactly as that for ATLS protocol to establish
priorities for management and is continued during transport until arrival at hospital of
definitive care.
Initial, but usually not definitive, management begins as problems are identified (as in
ATLS protocol). The first item evaluated is the airway; hard indications for intubation
include the following: Glasgow Coma Scale total score of less than 8 (inability to maintain

an airway), need for ventilation, potentially threatened airway (eg, inhalation injuries,
major facial injury, or expanding neck hematoma), or respiration rate less than 10
breaths per minute. Other indications are determined on a case-by-case basis.
The order of hemostasis is critical, as is stopping the bleeding. First, direct compression
is attempted; if this is futile or if bleeding is arterial, then the use of a tourniquet is
required. It is important that the time of tourniquet application is recorded so that
tourniquet time can be minimized if possible. Because tourniquets often are placed in
the field, communication with first responders is critical. Many tourniquet systems
currently have a place on the tourniquet on which to write the time of application with
the use of a marker.
Pelvic sheeting or pelvic binder application provides a pelvic splint stabilizing the forming
clot and allows for minimization of intrapelvic volume. Binders often are placed in the
field or on presentation to the trauma center if a volume-expanding pelvic ring injury is
suspected or confirmed. They limit the volume available for low-pressure bone and
venous bleeding. Binders do not control artery bleeding. The sheet or binder should be
placed at the level of the greater trochanters (Figure 1)

Secondary Survey
Performed after the primary survey has addressed immediate life-threatening injuries
Consists of a head-to-toe physical examination and detailed medical history (if available);
intended to diagnose and manage injuries that are not an immediate threat to life
Intravenous antibiotic agents should be administered to patients with open fractures as early
as possible. Early antibiotic agents have been shown to be the most crucial factor in limiting
infection rates after open fracture.14 Cefazolin is the preferred drug for all open fractures
unless contraindicated.14,15 The addition of an aminoglycoside, even for type III open
fractures, is controversial.
Advanced imaging studies
CT usually is performed as part of the secondary survey.
CT scans of the neck, entire chest, abdomen, pelvis, and extremities may be rapidly
performed with newer scanners and protocols.
Patient should be adequately stabilized hemodynamically to tolerate CT with minimal risk.

Secondary Survey
After the primary survey is complete and the patient’s immediate threats to life and limb
are stabilized, the secondary survey should take place. This is performed according to
the ATLS protocol, often during transport. This follows the AMPLE history (allergies to
medications, medications the patient is taking, pertinent medical history, last time eaten,
events leading to the injury).4
CT scans have largely replaced lateral cervical spine (C-Spine) radiographs.16 C-spine
precautions via a cervical collar should be maintained for patients who sustained blunt
trauma until proper imaging studies are obtained and physical examinations are
performed. Failure to obtain an AP pelvis radiograph before CT may result in delayed
diagnosis of hip dislocations and volume-expanding pelvic ring disruptions and
unnecessary repetition of CT and radiation exposure to the patient.
A Focused Assessment for the Sonographic Evaluation of the Trauma Patient (FAST) may
be used for patients in shock. Similar to radiographic evaluation, FAST is performed

quickly and may be performed in the trauma bay. FAST is accurate for detecting free
intraperitoneal fluid and for visualizing blood in the pericardial sac and dependent
regions of the abdomen, including the right and left upper quadrants and pelvis;
however, it cannot detect isolated bowel injuries and does not reliably detect
retroperitoneal injuries. MRI rarely is indicated in the early treatment of trauma patients.
Patients who have a cervical spine dislocation without progressive neurologic deficit may
benefit from MRI before closed reduction attempts; MRI may help identify interbody disk
herniation within the spinal canal that may cause neurologic impairment with closed
reduction.
Tertiary Survey
Performed when patients are awake, alert, and responsive and involves a detailed physical
examination and review of all imaging studies of the entire body to identify injuries not
previously identified. Although typically completed within 24 hours, completion may be
delayed because of patient condition.
Injuries to the hands and feet are the most common injuries missed in trauma patients.
Implementation of a tertiary survey has been shown to decrease missed injuries by 36%.17
Shock: Shock results in decreased end-organ perfusion. Hypovolemic shock is the most
common type of shock in trauma patients. Multiple forms of shock also may be present in a
single patient.

Shock resuscitation
Systolic blood pressure lower than 90 mm Hg on arrival is a risk factor for mortality.
Two large-bore intravenous lines should be obtained on arrival. Intraosseous access also
may be obtained for resuscitation.
Early transfusion via whole blood (1 unit of packed red blood cells: 1 unit of fresh frozen
plasma: 1 unit of platelets) decreases mortality.19
Rapid thrombelastography curves can be used to guide components of blood product
resuscitation.

Urine output also is used to monitor the adequacy of resuscitation.
Stop the bleed. Circumferential pelvic compression and tourniquets limit occult and visible
bleeding in the pelvis and extremities, respectively.
Hypothermia: Trauma patients are prone to hypothermia because of environmental exposure,
physiologic stress, and infusion of cold fluids.
Patients presenting with hypothermia require immediate intervention to prevent additional
physiologic stress and coagulopathy.
Iatrogenic hypothermia is preventable. Emergency department trauma bays and trauma
operating rooms should be kept warm to prevent hypothermia. Infused fluids and blood
products should be prewarmed.
Head-to-toe examination of a trauma patient is critical to avoid missing key injuries and sites
of blood loss. Immediately after this examination, the patient should be actively warmed to
prevent hypothermia.
Gradual rewarming is preferred to prevent dysrhythmia.
Coagulopathy: Hemorrhage control, balanced transfusion, and normothermia help avoid
preventable coagulopathy.
Balanced transfusions are key to avoiding hemodilution.
The combination of hypothermia, hemodilution, and acidosis may lead to coagulopathy, which
may worsen hemorrhage in a cyclical manner and lead to early mortality.20

Tertiary Survey
Although a primary survey is performed in the prehospital setting, the primary survey
should always be performed again after the patient arrives at the trauma center. As part
of continuous reassessment, these elements should be reevaluated frequently, and
treatment should change if any of the ABCDEs change as part of the patient’s clinical
course. A chest radiograph is key to identifying potential areas of bleeding but also is
important in evaluation of breathing and airway. Hypoxia may be caused by flail chest,
tension pneumothorax, or an open pneumothorax. During the secondary survey, the
importance of maintaining normothermia should not be ignored (recover and warm the
patient as quickly as possible).

Timely antibiotic prophylaxis and updating tetanus vaccination status should be
provided in patients with an open fracture.
Tertiary examinations are performed after the patient is stabilized and can, ideally,
participate in the examination. These are performed to identify injuries missed on the
initial primary and secondary surveys because these first two surveys are geared toward
more critical and potentially life-threatening injuries. The mindset of finding an injury
rather than confirming no other injury is present is important to identify injuries that, if
missed, may cause long-term morbidity. Twelve percent of injuries are missed in the first
24 hours.17
Evaluating the response to resuscitation is critical. Two liters of crystalloid are
administered first. Then non-responders, or transient responders, require transfusion.
Balanced product administration is advocated in massive transfusion situations with
regard to platelets, red blood cells, and crystalloid.
Differentiating the types of shock based on physiologic parameters is critical because
patients in neurogenic shock will not respond to resuscitation and require
pharmacologic and pressor support.
Physiologic Responses to Trauma
In the setting of trauma resulting in blood loss, tissue oxygenation decreases as circulating
blood volume decreases and as the body shunts blood flow to the most vital of structures.
This may lead to the lethal triad of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy.
As blood volume decreases from hemorrhage, oxygen delivery to tissues decreases, initiating
cellular anaerobic respiration to begin creating a state of acidosis.
This acidosis causes a decreased ability of platelets and clotting factors to function properly.
This inactivation of normal clotting leads to more blood loss, and this cycle may rapidly
advance itself to the point of no return.18 Eventually, this ineffectively perfused tissue leads to
hypothermia, further causing the cycle to spiral.
Several methods are used to measure the amount of acidosis and the amount of resuscitation
a patient requires.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:06 PM
AAOS | Evaluation of the Trauma Patient
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003016
17/35

Base deficit level is used to measure the amount of anaerobic acidosis that has and
continues to take place. Typically, a base deficit level of more than 5.5 mmol/L indicates a
patient requires continued resuscitation.
Lactate level is another indirect measure of this anaerobic process. Lactate is a product of
cellular anaerobic metabolism; lactate levels higher than 2.2 mmol/L indicate a patient who
may be considered under-resuscitated, and lactate levels higher than 4 represent a more
immediate resuscitation concern.
IL-6 is a cytokine produced by T cells, B cells, and endothelial cells. IL-6 levels are useful in that
they correlate with soft-tissue trauma, chest trauma, and ISS. IL-6 level is predictive of acute
respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), sepsis, and overall outcome.21 Several other
proinflammatory cytokines are observed in similar pathways, including IL-8 and IL-10.
This is a more indirect measure of trauma and is not directly produced by anaerobic
metabolism; however, it is a valuable indicator regarding the severity of soft-tissue trauma
that has occurred.
ARDS, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and multiple system organ failure
(MSOF) are sequelae of trauma-induced inflammation.
The timing of surgical treatment in polytrauma patients should be framed with regard to
their overall clinical picture.
SIRS is a clinical picture present in polytrauma patients that can be severely worsened by
inappropriately early surgical treatment that involves prolonged time in the operating room
or high blood loss.
Worsening SIRS may lead to MSOF and eventual death if appropriate resuscitation is not
performed before certain surgical interventions.

Physiologic Responses to Trauma
ARDS is a hyperinflammatory state in the lungs that is associated with rapidly increased
pulmonary edema associated with trauma. This often leads to decreased ability to
ventilate a patient, hypoxia, and pneumonia. ARDS classically is defined by the Berlin
definition.22 This definition includes the timing of onset within a week of injury or
worsening insult, bilateral opacities found on chest imaging studies (not otherwise
explained), and respiratory failure (not explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload).
Gradations of ARDS are defined in (Table 5).

SIRS is a systemic metabolic state that may be brought on by severe trauma and blood loss
characterized by hyperthermia or hypothermia (>38°C [100.4°F] or <36°C [96.8°F], respectively),
tachycardia (>90 bpm), tachypnea (>20 bpm), and elevated or suppressed white count (>12 ×
109/L or <4 × 109/L, respectively).4 Acute surgical management is associated with prolonged
surgical time and high blood loss and may cause an acute worsening of this response (the so-
called second hit), which may lead to MSOF and death.18 Acute trauma may initiate a SIRS
response, and aggressive surgical management may exacerbate it (the second hit).18
MSOF is characterized by two or more affected organ systems (pulmonary, cardiac, hepatic,
renal, hematologic, and neurologic) being damaged and often is the endpoint of worsening and
unmanaged SIRS. MSOF remains the primary reason for death in patients who survive the initial
phase of trauma.23 The Denver Multiple Organ Failure Score and the Sequential Organ Functional
Assessment score are the two most commonly used scoring tools that are validated in trauma
patients24,25 (Table 6).
These scoring systems are designed to evaluate for the presence and trend the severity of MSOF.
The goal of resuscitation is to prevent the onset and worsening severity of SIRS and MSOF and
ultimately prevent mortality in the in-hospital trauma phase. Clinicians should have an
understanding of these scoring systems because surgical decisions may have fatal consequences
in under-resuscitated or borderline patients.

Associated Injuries
Spine Injuries
Trauma patients are assumed to have spine injury until one is ruled out.
Cervical collars are placed, and log roll precautions for the thoracic and lumbar spine are in
effect.
Cervical spine injuries are ruled out via appropriate imaging studies (usually a CT scan) and
physical examination in an awake and alert patient.
Evaluation for thoracic and lumbar spine fracture via physical examination and imaging studies
of the spine
Beware of noncontiguous or multilevel spine injury.
Pelvic (Retroperitoneal) Versus Intra-abdominal Bleeding
These two injuries may coexist.
If diagnostic peritoneal lavage is performed in patients with a pelvic fracture, it should be
supraumbilical and performed early before the pelvic hematoma can track anteriorly. CT also
can be performed.
Circumferential pelvic compression with the use of a sheet or binder should be performed
early and should not be removed until the patient is adequately resuscitated.
If a sheet is used, holes may be cut in the sheet for groin access or placement of external

Pelvic (Retroperitoneal) Versus Intra-abdominal Bleeding
Pelvic binders, or sheeting, are highly useful tools to stabilize forming clot and decrease
intrapelvic volume, thereby contributing to resuscitative efforts. Although risks for soft-
tissue compromise exist, the benefits of maintaining a binder in an unstable patient
undergoing resuscitative efforts cannot be overstated. Pelvic packing and angiography
are associated with useful results. A key difference is that, in patients with venous
bleeding, angiography (and subsequent embolization) can only prevent inflow and
cannot directly halt pelvic extravasation from venous sources. Both strategies are
effective with the use of appropriate protocols.26
Head Injuries
Autoregulation of cerebral blood flow is altered after a head injury, and blood flow may
become dependent on mean arterial blood pressure.
Potentially preventable brain injury occurs if hypoperfusion or hypoxia arises after the initial
insult.
Poorly timed or poorly executed surgical management is a notable contributor to secondary
brain injury.
Management of head injuries in patients with multiple injuries is critical to their overall
outcomes. Intraoperative hypotension should be avoided in patients with head injuries
requiring intervention or monitoring because maintenance of cerebral blood flow may be
dysregulated and rely on mean arterial pressure in these patients.

Head Injuries
Whether early definitive fracture surgery has an adverse effect on neurologic outcome
remains a subject of debate. Maintenance of cerebral perfusion and oxygenation remain
the important goals during surgical management. Ventricular monitoring of intracranial
pressure is key in patients with more severe head injury. For fracture management in

Early surgical management that results in high-volume blood loss is contraindicated.
These patients require invasive monitoring to ensure that adequate cerebral blood flow
is maintained during surgical treatment. A detailed multidisciplinary discussion with
general surgery, neurosurgery, and orthopaedic surgery often helps chart the
appropriate course while minimizing risk to the patient.
Chest Injuries
Long bone and pelvic ring injuries often are observed in conjunction with chest injuries.
Rib fractures may indirectly impair gas exchange from pain (causing difficulty for patients to
inspire fully) and from loss of mechanical rib expansion (and paradoxical chest wall
movement), as observed in patients with flail chest.
Pulmonary contusions are a difficult injury to manage. They often are observed in patients
with rib fractures and may develop quickly and somewhat unexpectedly into life-threatening
situations.
The timing of long bone fixation in patients with substantial pulmonary injury remains an issue
of great clinical interest.
Sternal fractures and multiple rib fractures in addition to the mechanism of injury should
increase suspicion to evaluate for possible thoracic spine injuries.
CT reformatted images should be scrutinized to evaluate for thoracic spine injuries.
Spine lesions at multiple levels (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) are common, and, often, the
presence of one may mask another.

Abdominal Injuries
The goal of a primary survey is not to identify a specific abdominal injury but the presence of
any abdominal injury because they are exceedingly common in patients who sustain blunt or
penetrating trauma.
The use of CT scans and diagnostic peritoneal lavage associated with extremely high sensitivity
and specificity in detecting abdominal injuries.
More recently, the proliferation of ultrasonography has allowed for a FAST examination, which
is rapid and noninvasive and can be performed at the bedside, to become a common adjunct
to the primary survey for the detection of intra-abdominal injury.
Intra-abdominal injuries, mechanism of injury (eg, restrained motor vehicle collision), and
other spine fractures should increase suspicion for possible lumbar spine injuries.
CT reformatted images should be scrutinized to evaluate for lumbar spine injuries.
Spine lesions at multiple levels (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) are common, and, often, the
presence of one may mask another.

In polytrauma patients, injuries to abdominal visceral structures and lung injuries may
evolve over time. Therefore, reevaluation of polytrauma patients is critical, especially if
their clinical or hemodynamic status deteriorates. Communication between teams

prevent unnecessary morbidity and mortality while maximizing patient functional
outcomes. All members of the patient care team should maintain vigilance for the overall

injuries with deficits, joint dislocations with neurologic sequelae, joint dislocations
associated with osteonecrosis, fractures and dislocations with soft-tissue compromise
(eg, tongue-type calcaneus fractures), and open fractures. Historically, early total care
was used to manage all orthopaedic injuries acutely in hope that stabilizing the skeleton
would lead to improved rehabilitation of orthopaedic patients; however, this gave way to
damage-control orthopaedics in critically ill patients, which attempted to minimize the
second hit to the inflammatory cascade. Ideas of damage-control orthopaedics (eg,
provisional and rapid débridement and stabilization of injuries in critical patients)
continue to be used. The goal of damage-control orthopaedics is to prevent MSOF and
ARDS associated with early, invasive interventions in unstable, poorly resuscitated, or
borderline patients.
Indications initially used for damage-control orthopaedics were a lactate level higher
than 2 mmol/L, a systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mm Hg, hypothermia, and base
deficit level higher 4 mmol/L. The focus was early stabilization (within hours) of femoral
and tibial fractures via external fixation. The goal was to minimize the second hit of
surgery, with specific concern for ARDS and possible fat emboli, while providing
provisional skeletal stabilization.19,21
Recently, early appropriate care has attempted to definitively fix pelvic and acetabular
injuries and long bone fractures within the first 36 hours of admission. In a single-center
study, Vallier et al31 reported that a lactate level of less than 4 mmol/L, a pH level higher
than 7.25, and a base deficit level less than 5.5 mmol/L should be met before proceeding
with surgical management. The authors reported decreased hospital length of stay,
decreased morbidity, and decreased time in the ICU in patients who met these
parameters (Resource 2).
Irrigation and débridement of open fractures was historically thought to be necessary
within 6 hours; however, this has been shown to be unnecessary. Current guidelines
from the American College of Surgeons recommend débridement of open fractures
within 24 hours.32 This does not mean that these injuries should wait until the end of a
day of elective surgeries; instead, resuscitation of the patient should be performed and
appropriate imaging studies and treatment should be planned before management.

Special Considerations
Vascular Injury
The two pressing concerns regarding vascular injury in polytrauma patients are ischemia and
hemorrhage.
Irreversible muscle and nerve injury begin within 6 to 8 hours of ischemia.
Initial hemorrhage control, via direct pressure or tourniquet use, should be performed in the
field, ideally, and at the time of primary survey (C, for circulation in the ABCDEs)
Physical examination of the extremities to assess for adequate circulation is a key component
of the secondary survey.
Assessing for capillary refill, skin color, skin temperature, and presence of pulses should allow
for direction of additional diagnostics.
Several studies support the use of the ankle-brachial index in the lower extremity to rule out
substantial vascular injury.33,34
If additional concern exists, or the ankle-brachial index cannot be performed, CT angiography
and invasive angiography may aid in the evaluation and description of vascular injuries.
After a vascular injury has been identified, a cohesive, multidisciplinary plan to allow for rapid
stabilization and revascularization should begin. Time to revascularization is a critical
determinant of outcome.
Planning for management of vascular injuries should occur before the patient arrives. Having
treatment algorithms in place to standardize and expedite care is critical in the management
of these injuries.
In patients in extremis or who are borderline, revascularization and reconstruction is
contraindicated because of the added physiologic stress. Amputation may be lifesaving in
these patients.
Acute Compartment Syndrome
Acute compartment syndrome may lead to substantial morbidity if not promptly recognized.

Given that many polytrauma patients may have an impaired ability to participate in an
examination, concern for acute compartment syndrome in these patients should be extremely

If clinical signs or physical examination findings are concerning for compartment syndrome,
serial or continuous compartment monitoring may be performed to confirm or rule out this

If compartment syndrome develops, clear communication between services (ICU, general
surgery, and orthopaedic surgery) is critical in ensuring prompt and appropriate treatment of
the patient to minimize morbidity.

Special Considerations
Identification of vascular injuries is critical to resuscitation and optimization of outcomes
in polytrauma patients. Identifying and stopping hemorrhages via direct pressure and
the application of tourniquets, if appropriate, is a key component of a first responder’s
primary survey. After the patient has been transported to a trauma center, evaluation of
any extremity that has a tourniquet should be performed, and after stabilized, the
necessity of the tourniquet should be immediately evaluated. Tourniquets should be
loosened rather than removed; if bleeding begins, plans for direct control in the
operating room should rapidly be made. Time to restoration of blood flow in maintaining
limb viability is critical.21
Initial assessment of vascular status includes examination of skin color, temperature,
capillary refill, and pulses. In patients with an ischemic limb without hemorrhage, gross
alignment and any major joint dislocation should be restored and reduced; after this, a
prompt reexamination of vascular status should occur. If pulses are asymmetric, or
unable to be detected, Doppler examination and the ankle brachial index should be
performed. These are rapid and noninvasive methods that may be effective in early
identification of vascular injury.33,34 If restoration of limb alignment does not restore
blood flow, prompt evaluation by vascular surgery should occur, and the decision to
obtain additional imaging studies, outside the operating room or via on-table
angiography, should be made rapidly and in combination with all services treating the
patient.

Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical entity that is associated with substantial
morbidity if not recognized rapidly. Early signs of compartment syndrome include pain
out of proportion with the injury and pain with passive stretch of muscle compartments.
Later signs include paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, and loss of motor function. In
awake and alert patients, clinical examination is critical in the detection of acute
compartment syndrome. In obtunded patients, which often is observed with polytrauma
patients, this clinical assessment may be much more difficult and unreliable. In such
patients, serial or continuous compartment monitoring is indicated to evaluate for
compartment syndrome. A cut off value difference of 30 mm Hg classically is used for
the diagnosis of compartment syndrome via pressure monitoring (this represents the
difference between the measured diastolic pressure and the measured compartment
pressure).35 Although recent data has resulted in concerns that this may lead to too high
of a false-positive rate,36 given the sequelae of missed compartment syndrome and the
difficulty of evaluating obtunded patients, this false-positive rate likely is acceptable to
prevent a missed diagnosis. Evaluation for compartment syndrome takes place, and
regular reexaminations are necessary because compartment syndrome may evolve over
time; one physical examination or one compartment measurement is insufficient to rule
out compartment syndrome. After a diagnosis is made, prompt management via
compartment releases is necessary to prevent myonecrosis and its associated morbidity.
